    How models learn: loss & gradient descent

    After this lesson you can describe, precisely, the loop that turns "nudge the knobs" into an algorithm — loss, gradient, learning rate — and explain what an epoch and a minibatch are.

    Level: beginner Read time: ~16 min Prerequisites: What is a model? Updated: 13 Nov 2026

    In the last lesson we said training is a loop: predict, measure how wrong you are, nudge the parameters to be less wrong, repeat. That word "nudge" was doing a lot of work. This lesson replaces it with an actual algorithm — gradient descent — which is, with surprisingly few changes, how every model in this course is trained.

    Step one: turn "wrong" into a number

    You can't minimize something you can't measure. So the first ingredient is a loss function: it takes the model's prediction and the true answer and returns a single number that is large when the prediction is bad and small when it's good.

    For the house-price model, a natural loss is the squared error: take the gap between predicted and actual price, and square it. Predict 250k when the truth is 240k and the loss for that example is (250k − 240k)² = 100,000,000. Square it so over- and under-shooting both count as positive error, and bigger mistakes are penalized harder. The loss over a dataset is just the average over all examples.

    Different tasks use different loss functions — language models use cross-entropy, which we'll meet in Track 1 — but the role is always the same: one number, smaller is better.

    The loss is a landscape over the parameters

    Here is the key mental shift. Hold the data fixed and think of the loss as a function of the parameters. For the two-knob house model, every choice of (w, b) produces some average loss. Picture that as a landscape: the two knobs are your east–west and north–south position, and the loss is the altitude. Training is the search for the lowest valley.

    Key idea

    Training does not search over predictions; it searches over parameters. The data defines the shape of the landscape; the parameters are where you're standing on it.

    Gradient descent: roll downhill

    How do you get to the valley when you can only feel the ground right under your feet? You measure the slope and step downhill. In more than one dimension the slope is called the gradient: it points in the direction the loss increases fastest. So to decrease the loss, you step in the opposite direction. That's the whole idea — gradient descent:

    for each step:

      prediction = model(inputs) # forward pass

      loss = loss_fn(prediction, truth)

      gradient = how loss changes w.r.t. each parameter

      parameter = parameter − learning_rate × gradient # the nudge

    That last line is "the nudge," now precise: move every parameter a little, against its gradient. Repeat thousands of times and you descend into a valley of low loss.

    One step, with real numbers

    Take a one-knob model prediction = w × x, one example x = 2 with true answer y = 10, a starting value w = 3 and a learning rate of 0.05. The loss is the squared error (w × x − y)².

    • Forward pass: prediction 3 × 2 = 6, loss (6 − 10)² = 16.
    • Gradient: the slope of (wx − y)² with respect to w is 2(wx − y) × x = 2 × (−4) × 2 = −16. Negative means "increasing w lowers the loss".
    • Nudge: w = 3 − 0.05 × (−16) = 3.8. New prediction 7.6, new loss (7.6 − 10)² = 5.76. One step cut the loss from 16 to 5.76.

    A training framework does exactly this, except it computes the gradient automatically (backpropagation, next lesson) for every parameter at once.

    The learning rate: how big a step

    The learning rate is the multiplier on the step. It is the single most important number you'll tune. Too small and training crawls, taking forever to reach the valley. Too large and you leap clear over the valley and bounce around — or diverge entirely, with the loss shooting to infinity. Typical values for fine-tuning are small: 2e-4 (0.0002) is common for LoRA fine-tuning, and full fine-tuning uses smaller values still, often around 1e-5 to 5e-5. Both are starting points that people tune, not laws; Track 1's learning-rate lesson explains why.

    Common failure

    A loss that explodes to NaN after a few steps most often means the learning rate is too high (other causes: fp16 overflow, a bad row, or a batch where every label is masked). A loss that barely moves means it's too low. Reading the loss curve is a skill you'll use constantly.

    Minibatches and epochs

    Computing the gradient over the entire dataset for every step is accurate but slow. Instead we use a minibatch: a small random handful of examples (say 8 or 32). Each step computes the gradient on one minibatch and updates. Because the batch is a random sample, the gradient is a noisy estimate of the true one — hence the name stochastic gradient descent (SGD). The noise is mostly harmless and often seems to help: models trained with smaller, noisier batches tend to generalise a little better (Keskar et al. 2016, arXiv 1609.04836). That is an empirical observation, not a theorem.

    What real training uses: AdamW

    Plain SGD uses one learning rate for every parameter. Almost every language-model run today uses AdamW instead (Kingma & Ba 2014, arXiv 1412.6980; Loshchilov & Hutter 2017, arXiv 1711.05101). It is still "step against the gradient", with two additions: it keeps a running average of recent gradients (momentum, which smooths the noisy steps) and scales each parameter's step by how large that parameter's gradients usually are, so rarely-updated parameters still move. The "W" is weight decay, a gentle pull of every weight toward zero. The cost is memory: AdamW stores two extra numbers per trained parameter, which matters a lot in Track 1's memory math.

    One full pass through all the training data is an epoch. You typically train for a few epochs. "Train for 3 epochs with batch size 8" means: shuffle the data, walk through it in groups of 8 updating each time, and do that whole walk 3 times.

    Does it actually find the bottom?

    In theory the landscape can have dips that aren't the deepest valley (local minima) and flat plateaus. In millions of dimensions most flat spots turn out to be saddle points, downhill in some direction, rather than true local minima (Dauphin et al. 2014, arXiv 1406.2572). In practice, for the large models we train, gradient descent reliably finds parameter settings that are good enough. That is an observed fact, not a proven one, and deep learning runs on it. You won't be proving convergence; you'll be watching a loss curve go down and stop when it stops improving.

    Low training loss is not the goal: overfitting

    The loss you minimise is measured on the training examples. What you actually want is a model that does well on examples it has never seen. So you hold some examples back as a validation set and measure the loss on them too, without training on them. Early on both curves fall together. If you keep going, the model starts memorising quirks of the training rows: training loss keeps falling while validation loss flattens and then rises. That gap is overfitting, and the usual fix is to stop near the lowest validation loss, train for fewer epochs, or get more varied data.

    This is why every serious project keeps data the model never trains on, and why later lessons insist on a separate test set (overfitting and loss curves goes deeper).

    That's the engine. Everything else — neural networks, Transformers, LoRA — changes what the model computes and which parameters exist, but the training loop stays this loop. Next we look at the kind of model that makes language possible: the neural network.

    Recap

    • Training minimises one number, the loss, by stepping every parameter against its gradient; the learning rate sets the step size.
    • Real runs use minibatches and AdamW, which adds momentum and per-parameter step sizes to the same idea.
    • Training loss alone is not the goal: watch a held-back validation loss to catch overfitting.

    Try it (5 minutes)

    Same one-knob model prediction = w × x and squared-error loss. Now x = 3, y = 6, start at w = 1. Do one gradient step with learning rate 0.05, then redo it with learning rate 0.5. What happens to the loss each time?

    Show answer

    Start: prediction 3, loss (3 − 6)² = 9, gradient 2 × (3 − 6) × 3 = −18. With learning rate 0.05: w = 1 + 0.9 = 1.9, prediction 5.7, loss 0.09, a big improvement (the best value is w = 2). With learning rate 0.5: w = 1 + 9 = 10, prediction 30, loss 576. The step leapt clear over the valley and the loss got 64 times worse. That is the "too high" learning rate from the warning above, in two lines of arithmetic.

    Key terms

    Loss function
    A function returning one number measuring how wrong the model's predictions are; smaller is better.
    Gradient
    The direction (over all parameters) in which the loss increases fastest; we step the opposite way.
    Gradient descent
    Repeatedly nudging parameters against the gradient to reduce loss.
    Learning rate
    The step-size multiplier; too high diverges, too low crawls.
    Minibatch / SGD
    Estimating the gradient on a small random batch each step (stochastic gradient descent).
    Epoch
    One complete pass through the training dataset.
    AdamW
    The default optimizer for language models: gradient descent with momentum, per-parameter step sizes and weight decay.
    Validation set / overfitting
    Examples held back from training to measure generalisation; overfitting is when training loss keeps falling while validation loss rises.
